_note: Standard textile wet-processing curriculum knowledge (dye chemistry, machine theory, fastness testing) — the same status as academy-engine.js's knitting theory: general engineering knowledge, not tied to a single external source, and never carrying an outbound citation (see knitadvisor-no-source-links). Complements dyeing-engine.js's real recipe cards and dyeing-faults-engine.js's fault/QC layer with the 'why', not just the 'what'.

dye_classes.name: Reactive Dyes
dye_classes.mechanism: The dye molecule carries a reactive group (e.g. a chlorotriazine or vinyl sulphone) that forms a genuine covalent bond with the -OH groups of cellulose under alkaline conditions — the dye becomes chemically part of the fibre, not just physically trapped in it. This is why reactive dyeing gives the best wash fastness of any water-soluble dye class on cotton.
key_chemicals: Common salt or Glauber's salt (exhausting electrolyte)
advantages: Excellent wash and rub fastness once fixed
Bright, wide shade range
Works at moderate temperature (no pressure vessel needed)
limitations: Dye hydrolysis in the alkaline bath is unavoidable — typically 20-30% of the dye reacts with water instead of the fibre and is wasted, never fixing
Hydrolysed dye must be washed off with heavy soaping/rinsing, which is exactly why unfinished soaping causes rubbing-fastness failures
High-salt effluent is a real wastewater burden (see the salt-comparison data in dyeing-faults-engine.js)
No affinity for polyester — a poly/cotton blend always needs a second dye class

dye_classes.name: Disperse Dyes
dye_classes.mechanism: These dyes are barely water-soluble — they're applied as a fine aqueous dispersion (hence the name) and dye hydrophobic synthetic fibres by dissolving INTO the fibre polymer itself as the fibre softens under heat, rather than by any chemical bond. This is why high temperature (or a carrier chemical) is essential: below the fibre's glass transition point, the dye simply cannot diffuse in.

typical_conditions.temp_c: 125-135 (HTHP/pressure method) or ~100 with a carrier chemical at atmospheric pressure

key_chemicals: Dispersing agent (keeps the dye particles suspended)
Carrier chemical (atmospheric method only) or reduction-clearing agent (caustic soda + sodium hydrosulphite) post-dyeing
advantages: Only practical class for polyester
Good to excellent light and sublimation fastness when properly cleared
HTHP method needs no carrier chemical (avoids carrier odour/toxicity concerns)
limitations: HTHP needs a pressure-rated jet machine — real capital cost
Unfixed surface dye must be reduction-cleared or it crocks/rubs off and bleeds on later heat-setting
The carrier (atmospheric) method's carrier chemicals are often odorous and some are restricted for effluent/health reasons
No affinity for cellulose — useless alone on 100% cotton

dye_classes.name: Vat Dyes
dye_classes.mechanism: The dye is insoluble in water in its normal form. It is first chemically reduced (with sodium hydrosulphite/hydros + caustic soda) into a soluble, substantive 'leuco' form that has affinity for cellulose and penetrates the fibre. Exposing it to air or a mild oxidiser (oxidation step) converts it back to its original, large, completely insoluble pigment form — now locked physically inside the fibre. Indigo (denim) works on exactly this vat-dye chemistry.

typical_conditions.ph: highly alkaline during vatting (from caustic soda)
typical_conditions.time_min: 20-40 per vatting cycle, often repeated (denim ring-dyeing uses multiple dip-oxidation cycles)

key_chemicals: An oxidising agent or simply atmospheric oxygen
Soaping agent (final boil to develop full, true shade)
advantages: The best overall wash AND light fastness of any dye class on cellulose — this is why vat dyes, not reactives, are used where fastness cannot be compromised
The controlled, incomplete penetration used deliberately in denim gives the classic indigo 'ring-dyed' fade effect
limitations: The most expensive and chemically complex process of the cellulosic dye classes
Hydrosulphite handling carries real odour and effluent-oxygen-demand concerns
Colour range is narrower and duller than reactive dyes for many shades
Multiple vatting/oxidation cycles for full shade depth cost real production time

dye_classes.name: Direct Dyes
dye_classes.mechanism: Long, linear dye molecules with natural substantivity for cellulose — they align along and hydrogen-bond to the cellulose chain directly from a near-boiling salt bath, no fixing chemical required. This is the simplest of all the cellulose dye classes, which is exactly its weakness: the bond is physical (hydrogen bonding + van der Waals), not chemical, so it is inherently reversible.
key_chemicals: A cationic fixing agent after dyeing, if wet fastness must be improved
advantages: Cheapest and simplest cellulose dyeing process — low energy, no pressure vessel, minimal chemistry
Wide, economical shade range for low-durability-requirement goods
limitations: Poor wet/wash fastness without an after-fixing treatment — the dye is not chemically bonded and will bleed
Not suitable for garments needing repeated laundering unless fixed
Generally duller shades than reactive or vat for the same colour

dye_classes.name: Acid Dyes
dye_classes.mechanism: Applied from an acidic bath (acetic or formic acid) onto protein/polyamide fibres, where the dye's anionic (acid) groups form an ionic bond with the fibre's cationic amino (-NH3+) groups. The strength of this bond, and therefore the fastness achieved, depends heavily on matching dye type (levelling / milling / super-milling acid dyes) to the fastness needed.

typical_conditions.temp_c: 80-100 for wool/nylon, cooler for silk to protect the fibre's handle

key_chemicals: Ammonium sulphate (buffers pH rise during dyeing)
advantages: Bright, clear shades on protein and polyamide fibres
Good to very good fastness available (milling/super-milling grades) when the right sub-class is chosen
limitations: No affinity whatsoever for cellulosic fibres — irrelevant to 100% cotton
Fast-striking acid dyes need real leveling-agent control or they dye unevenly, patchy exactly like the fabric faults this codebase already tracks
Wool needs careful temperature control to avoid felting/fibre damage during dyeing

dye_classes.name: Basic (Cationic) Dyes
dye_classes.mechanism: Cationic (positively charged) dye molecules bond ionically to the anionic acid-group sites built into acrylic fibre during its manufacture. The affinity is so strong and fast that, without control, the dye 'strikes' (exhausts) almost instantly and unevenly.

typical_conditions.temp_c: 85-100 (often with a slow, controlled temperature ramp)

key_chemicals: A cationic retarder — essential, not optional, to slow the initial strike rate
advantages: Extremely bright, vivid, high-strength shades — brighter than almost any other dye class on the fibres it fits
limitations: Only works on acrylic and specially modified fibres — no use on standard polyester, cotton, or wool
Without a retarder, the fast strike rate produces exactly the kind of unlevel/patchy dyeing this codebase's fault database already documents for other causes
Historically weaker lightfastness than other classes, though modern basic dyes for acrylic have narrowed this gap considerably

dye_classes.name: Sulphur Dyes
dye_classes.mechanism: Like vat dyes, sulphur dyes are insoluble pigments made soluble by reduction (traditionally with sodium sulphide) into a form with affinity for cellulose, then re-oxidised back to the insoluble pigment inside the fibre after dyeing. Chemically related to vat dyeing but cheaper and chemically cruder.
key_chemicals: Sodium sulphide (traditional reducing agent) or a lower-sulphide alternative
A thorough acid/oxidation wash to remove residual sulphur compounds
advantages: The cheapest route to deep, wash-fast blacks, navies and khakis on cotton
Good wash fastness for the cost
limitations: Residual sulphur left in the fabric from incomplete after-treatment causes 'sulphur tendering' — slow acid-catalysed fibre damage and strength loss over storage/shelf life if the neutralisation step is skipped or rushed
Duller shades than reactive or vat dyes — not suitable where a bright, saturated colour is required
Traditional sodium sulphide reduction carries real effluent/odour concerns, pushing many mills toward lower-sulphide reducing systems

machines.name: Jet Dyeing Machine
machines.form: Rope form — fabric circulates as a rope, driven by a high-velocity jet of dye liquor rather than a reel alone
machines.liquor_ratio_range: 1:4 to 1:10 (some modern low-liquor-ratio jets go tighter still)
machines.typical_use: Knit fabric (jersey, interlock, rib) — the dominant machine for HTHP disperse dyeing of polyester knits and reactive dyeing of cotton knits
advantages: Low liquor ratio saves water, energy, and chemical cost per kg dyed
Sealed, pressurisable vessel makes 130C HTHP disperse dyeing possible
Good liquor circulation gives level dyeing at speed
limitations: Rope form and jet impact can cause crease/rope marks and crow's-feet on delicate or loosely-constructed knits if speed/pressure aren't matched to the fabric — exactly the fault mechanism in this codebase's crack/rope-mark and crow's-feet entries
Not suitable for open-width-sensitive wovens that must never be creased

machines.name: Winch / Soft-Flow Machine
machines.form: Rope form, atmospheric pressure, fabric driven mainly by a reel (winch) with liquor assist in soft-flow variants
machines.liquor_ratio_range: 1:8 to 1:15 — notably higher than a modern jet
machines.typical_use: Delicate or lightweight fabrics that a full jet's mechanical action would damage; atmospheric-only processes (can't do HTHP disperse dyeing without a pressure vessel)
advantages: Gentler mechanical action than a jet — better for delicate knits/wovens
Simpler, lower-cost machine than a pressurised jet
limitations: Higher liquor ratio than a jet means more water, energy and chemical per kg
Atmospheric-only, so it cannot run true HTHP disperse dyeing on polyester without a carrier chemical

machines.name: Jigger
machines.form: Open-width (not rope) — fabric runs back and forth between two rollers through a stationary dye bath
machines.liquor_ratio_range: 1:3 to 1:5 — one of the lowest liquor ratios of any batch machine, because the fabric itself displaces most of the liquor volume
machines.typical_use: Open-width-sensitive woven fabrics (denim, twill) that must never be creased or rope-marked
advantages: Very low liquor ratio
No rope-form crease risk at all — the fabric never bunches
limitations: Batch-to-batch shade variation is a real, well-documented jigger risk if batching time/heating uniformity isn't controlled tightly (see the fault database's dark/light-selvedge and batch-variation entries)
Not usable for knit fabrics, which distort badly under open-width tension

machines.name: Cold Pad-Batch
machines.form: Continuous, open-width — fabric is padded (impregnated under nip rollers) with dye+alkali, then rolled onto a beam and rotated slowly at ambient temperature for hours
machines.liquor_ratio_range: Effectively ~1:1 (a pad, not a bath) — the lowest of any dyeing method
machines.typical_use: High-volume woven cotton reactive dyeing where energy cost matters most
advantages: By far the lowest water and energy use of any reactive dyeing route — no heating at all during fixation
High production speed for the padding step itself
limitations: Fixation happens over 4-24 hours of slow batch rotation — the batch roll MUST rotate evenly or the dye migrates/pools, producing exactly the tailing and end-to-end shade variation this process is notorious for
Padding uniformity across the full fabric width has to be precise; the fault database's roller/padder-related shade-variation causes apply directly here
Needs floor space and time for the batching step that an exhaust machine doesn't

machines.name: Pad-Steam (Continuous)
machines.form: Continuous, open-width — padding immediately followed by a steamer for fixation, rather than a long cold batch
machines.liquor_ratio_range: Effectively ~1:1 at the pad, same as pad-batch
machines.typical_use: High-volume continuous dyeing where pad-batch's multi-hour batching time is a production bottleneck
advantages: Continuous, fast — no multi-hour batching wait
Low liquor ratio like pad-batch
limitations: Steamer temperature/humidity/dwell-time uniformity across the full width is critical — an uneven steamer reproduces the same shade-variation risk pad-batch has from uneven batching
Higher energy cost than pad-batch, since the steaming step actively heats the fabric instead of relying on ambient-temperature time

machines.name: Beam Dyeing Machine
machines.form: Fabric (or yarn) wound onto a perforated beam; liquor is pumped radially through the wound layers rather than the fabric moving through the liquor
machines.typical_use: Fabrics too delicate or crease-sensitive for any rope or reel action at all
advantages: Zero rope/reel mechanical stress on the fabric — the fabric itself never moves
limitations: Even liquor flow through every wound layer is essential — a channelled or uneven wind produces severe layer-to-layer shade variation with no rope action to average it out
Winding the beam evenly is itself a real skill/setup cost

process_flows.name: Cotton Knit — Reactive Exhaust Dyeing (Jet/Soft-Flow)

steps.name: Pretreatment
steps.detail: Scouring (removes natural waxes/impurities) and bleaching (removes natural colour/seed-coat fragments) in the same or separate bath, so the fibre is uniformly absorbent before any dye goes in.

steps.name: Dye addition
steps.detail: Dissolved, filtered dye added at a steadily increasing rate (a rapid dump is a documented cause of uneven dyeing) at moderate temperature.

steps.name: Salt addition
steps.detail: Electrolyte (common or Glauber's salt) added in stages to exhaust the dye from the bath onto the fibre, without yet fixing it chemically.

steps.name: Alkali addition / fixation
steps.detail: Soda ash (or caustic for some dye types) raised to pH ~11 to trigger the actual covalent fixation reaction onto cellulose; held at this pH/temperature for the fixation time.

steps.name: Rinsing
steps.detail: Hot then cold rinses to remove the bulk of unfixed, hydrolysed dye and salt before soaping.

steps.name: Neutralisation
steps.detail: Acetic acid brings the bath back to neutral/mildly acidic pH.

steps.name: Soaping
steps.detail: A near-boil wash with a soaping agent — this is the step that removes the hydrolysed dye a reactive bath inevitably produces; skipping or shortening it is a direct cause of poor rub/wash fastness.

steps.name: Softening & drying
steps.detail: Softener applied, then dried to final moisture content.

notes: This is the flow the shade-variation QC checklist in dyeing-faults-engine.js is built around — its five stages (preparatory/dyeing/finishing/soaping/machinery) map directly onto steps 1, 2-4, 6, 7 and the machine itself.

process_flows.name: Polyester — HTHP Disperse Dyeing (Jet)

steps.name: Pretreatment
steps.detail: Scouring and, for many polyester fabrics, heat-setting before dyeing to stabilise dimensions so the dyeing heat itself doesn't cause further shrinkage/distortion.

steps.name: Dye addition
steps.detail: Dispersed dye, dispersing agent and levelling agent added at moderate starting temperature (~50-60C), pH adjusted to ~4.5-5 with acetic acid.

steps.name: Controlled heating to HTHP
steps.detail: Temperature raised gradually (a fast ramp risks unlevel dyeing) to 125-135C under pressure, held for 30-60 minutes — this is the step that actually diffuses dye into the polyester polymer.

steps.name: Cooling & reduction clearing
steps.detail: After cooling, a caustic soda + sodium hydrosulphite wash strips unfixed dye sitting on the fibre surface — without this step, surface dye crocks/rubs off and can migrate/stain during later heat-setting.

steps.name: Neutralisation & soaping
steps.detail: Neutralise the caustic, then a soaping/rinse sequence.

steps.name: Drying & heat-set finishing
steps.detail: Final dry and, often, a finishing heat-set pass.

notes: The reduction-clearing step (4) is the single most common thing skipped or shortened under time pressure, and it is the direct cause of most disperse-dyed crocking/rubbing-fastness complaints.

process_flows.name: Poly/Cotton Blend — Two-Part (Disperse + Reactive)
process_flows.fabric_type: CVC / PC blended knit or woven

steps.name: Pretreatment
steps.detail: Scouring/bleaching as for 100% cotton, since the cotton component still needs to be absorbent.

steps.name: Disperse dyeing (polyester component)
steps.detail: Run the HTHP disperse process above first — the polyester component is dyed while the cotton component is largely unaffected by disperse dye at this stage.

steps.name: Reduction clearing
steps.detail: Essential here even more than on 100% polyester — surface disperse dye left on the COTTON portion (which has no affinity for it) will stain badly if not cleared before the reactive step.

steps.name: Reactive dyeing (cotton component)
steps.detail: Run the standard reactive exhaust process (salt, then alkali fixation) to dye the cotton component to match or complement the polyester shade.

steps.name: Final soaping, neutralisation, softening, drying
steps.detail: As in the single-fibre flows, but now clearing residues from BOTH dye classes.

notes: This is exactly why dyeing-engine.js's matchDyeingRecipe() treats is_two_part as decisive when choosing between candidate recipes — a two-part fabric genuinely runs two dyeing processes end to end, at real extra chemical and time cost versus a single-fibre fabric of the same shade.

process_flows.name: Woven Cotton — Cold Pad-Batch Reactive Dyeing

steps.name: Pretreatment
steps.detail: Scouring/bleaching in open-width, as the fabric will run open-width through the entire process.

steps.name: Padding
steps.detail: Fabric impregnated with dye + alkali together (unlike exhaust dyeing, both go on at once) under nip rollers at ambient temperature — nip pressure evenness across the full width is critical.

steps.name: Batching
steps.detail: The padded fabric is rolled onto a beam wrapped to prevent drying out, then rotated slowly at ambient temperature for 4-24 hours while the alkali fixes the dye onto the cellulose.

steps.name: Washing-off
steps.detail: Cold then hot rinse and soap to remove unfixed dye and alkali, same purpose as exhaust dyeing's soaping step.

steps.name: Drying & finishing
steps.detail: Standard drying/finishing.

notes: No heating step exists anywhere in this flow except the wash-off — the entire energy saving versus exhaust dyeing comes from fixation happening at ambient temperature over time instead of at high temperature quickly.
Batch rotation must never stop during the batching stage: a stalled roll lets liquor migrate downward under gravity, which is the direct cause of top-to-bottom shade variation on a pad-batch roll.

process_flows.name: Denim — Indigo Rope (Vat-Class) Dyeing

steps.name: Vatting (reduction)
steps.detail: Indigo, insoluble as a pigment, is reduced with sodium hydrosulphite + caustic soda into its soluble, yellow-green leuco form in the dye vat.

steps.name: Dip
steps.detail: The warp rope is dipped into the leuco vat, where the soluble leuco-indigo penetrates the outer layers of the yarn.

steps.name: Oxidation (air exposure)
steps.detail: On exposure to air, the leuco form re-oxidises back to insoluble indigo pigment, trapped physically where it penetrated — this is the step that actually develops the blue colour, not the dip itself.

steps.name: Repeat dip-oxidise cycles
steps.detail: Steps 2-3 are repeated multiple times (commonly 6-8+ passes) to build up shade depth, since each single dip only deposits a thin layer.

notes: Indigo deliberately does NOT fully penetrate the yarn core — this incomplete, surface-concentrated dyeing ("ring dyeing") is not a defect here, it's the entire reason denim can be abraded/washed to reveal the undyed core for fade effects. Judging indigo dyeing by full-penetration standards used for other vat-dyed cellulosics would be a real misapplication of that QC criterion.

fastness.summary: Fastness testing measures how well a dyeing survives real-world stresses (washing, rubbing, light, sweat) — it is the pass/fail gate a recipe/process choice is ultimately judged against, independent of how good the shade looks fresh off the machine.

grey_scale_change.purpose: Grades how much the DYED fabric itself has changed (faded/altered) after a fastness test, by visual comparison against a standard set of grey-toned reference pairs.
grey_scale_change.scale: 1 (severe change) to 5 (no perceptible change), with half-grades (e.g. 4-5) commonly used
grey_scale_change.typical_pass_bar: 4 or better for wash fastness on garments expected to withstand repeated laundering; lower grades are acceptable for single-wear or non-garment textiles

grey_scale_staining.purpose: Grades how much dye has bled from the dyed fabric onto an adjacent piece of undyed fabric during the same test — a separate scale from colour CHANGE, because a fabric can hold its own shade well while still staining its neighbour badly.
grey_scale_staining.typical_pass_bar: 4 or better, especially for garments packed/stored against light-coloured linings or other garments

test_types.name: Wash fastness
test_types.purpose: Simulates repeated home/industrial laundering — the single most commonly specified test for garment fabric, and the test reactive-dye soaping (see the cotton-knit-reactive flow) exists specifically to pass.

test_types.name: Rubbing / crocking fastness
test_types.purpose: Measures dye transfer from simple dry or wet rubbing against another surface — tested separately dry and wet because wet crocking is almost always worse, and is the test directly referenced in this codebase's salt-comparison data.

test_types.name: Light fastness
test_types.purpose: Measures fading under prolonged light (sunlight or a xenon-arc lamp simulating it) exposure — vat dyes' well-known light-fastness advantage over reactive dyes on cotton is measured by exactly this test.

test_types.name: Perspiration fastness
test_types.purpose: Measures colour change/staining after exposure to simulated acidic and alkaline sweat — particularly relevant to garments worn against skin.
